newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch funds like home market but seek to diversify.
newsitem.headline: Dutch funds like home market but seek to diversify.

text.p: Dutch institutional investors say five years of solid outperformance by the Amsterdam stock exchange have given their equity portfolios a welcome boost, but many expect more modest returns in the years ahead.
In local currency terms the AEX share index has risen 236 percent since the end of 1992, eclipsing New York where the Dow has risen 144 percent and Frankfurt which is up 174 percent.
Dutch managers say domestic equities will continue to reward investors who take a long-term view but many are also pressing ahead with further diversification beyond their home market.
"We don't expect a dramatic decline, because there's hardly any alternative for equities with these sort of interest rates," said Frits Moolhuizen of ING Investment Management.
"Earnings momentum is still very strong, but we don't expect the same sort of returns in the next five years as we've seen in the past five," he said.

Moolhuizen, responsible for some 30 billion guilders ($14.6 billion) worth of equity investments around the world, said valuations for Dutch shares had risen dramatically in recent years and were currently discounting a lot of good news which was yet to come.
Rob Lambregts of the railway workers pension fund SPF said the current environment continued to look friendly for equities.
"All of the indicators for the share market -- the economy, profits, interest rates -- still seem to be positive, so I'm not really afraid that we're heading for a big crash," he said.
Lambregts said nobody should be surprised, however, if at some point the AEX fell 100 points in a few days time.
"But that would by no means signal that the positive climate for shares had suddenly disappeared," he said.

SPF, with investments worth 14.6 billion guilders at the end of last year, gained autonomy from the Dutch government at the end of 1993 and since then it has gradually sought to invest more of its money in equities and outside the Netherlands.
Under the old regime it could invest only in Dutch assets, with a combined 25 percent ceiling on equities and property.

By the end of 1996, some 24 percent of the fund's assets were non-Dutch and equities made up 39 percent of the portfolio -- though these figures are planned to rise to around 40 percent and 50 percent respectively.

Lambregts said the rapid appreciation of Dutch share prices had worked against the fund's plans to obtain a wider geographic spread of assets and seemed likely to bring about the desired level of equity holdings much sooner than expected.

Previously SPF had planned to pursue its goals by using investment income and money raised by selling bonds to step up its investment in foreign equities, however the relentless rise of Dutch share prices may force a rethink.
"We are starting to ask ourselves whether we should perhaps sell off some of our Dutch shareholdings," Lambregts said.

Moolhuizen at ING said the Dutch component of the equity portfolios he managed remained fairly steady around 30 percent, though this year he had reduced holdings in the Netherlands and some Asian countries slightly in favour of the United States.
"We've also increased our exposure to Latin American and East European markets such as Russia," he said.
Moolhuizen said holdings in these emerging markets remained modest -- about one percent for each region -- for the time being but would probably rise further in the future.

Asked to explain the Dutch stock market's strong performance in recent years, Moolhuizen pointed to the international character of leading Dutch companies and the relatively high weighting of fast-growing service industry stocks in the AEX.
However, given the Dutch market's rapid ascent to date, annual returns on Dutch equities in the next few years were more likely to be below 10 percent a year than above it, he added.
